title: The Gestures We’ve Forgotten
text:
This is an edition of Ordinary Extraordinary, Ian Bogost’s guide to making everyday life vivid. Sign up for the newsletter here. 

 On a recent trip to the local planetarium, I visited the gift shop to waste some time before the star show. Inside, I found one of those penny-press souvenir machines, the kind that turns an ordinary cent (plus two quarters as a fee) into a copper oval with an impression of the attraction.

 I don’t typically carry cash of any kind, let alone coins. But the device had a giant geared crank to do the pressing, and I found myself turning it even though I didn’t pay for a pressed penny. The gears ratcheted gratifyingly, but the cranking action on its own also felt good.

 Something about cranking is really delightful. But like pennies, cranking has been almost completely eliminated from everyday life. Standing there in the planetarium, cranking the empty penny press like a maniac, I pondered all the mechanisms I had cranked in the past. Paper-towel dispensers used to crank. I remember one in particular, pure white with a small chrome crank that spun fast and free, releasing as little or as much towel as I desired. A sound accompanied the act, as the cylinder whirled with a rhythmic whoong, whoong . That’s the stuff, right there.

 If you are old enough to remember, other cranks will come to mind. Car windows used to crank open, but not anymore; Jeep, the last holdout, eliminated manual windows in its 2025 models. In homes and classrooms, a crankable, wall-mounted pencil sharpener was standard, until mechanical pencils and electric sharpeners came along. Rewinding a film camera required cranking. Tall, restaurant-style “Tell me when” pepper grinders still have cranks, but few home-dining grinders do anymore. Nor do other manual kitchen gadgets: flour sifters, egg beaters, ice-cream makers, or apple peelers.

 Further back, cash registers had a crank, which the cashier would rotate to tally a total after entering an item’s price. Also telephone magnetos (used to ring the operator), car engines (before electric starters), hospital beds, well buckets, clothes wringers, turn-of-the-century penny-arcade Mutoscopes, Victorian cuff-rippling fluting irons, and Occitan-folk-music-emitting hurdy-gurdies.

 Cranking has not left us entirely. Boat winches and trailer jacks still crank, although predominantly by motor now. Fishing reels crank. So do music boxes. After returning from the star show, I searched my home for any that remained, and indeed, cranks still find a way: in hose reels, patio umbrellas, casement-window handles, can openers.

 The decline of cranks can be attributed mostly to electrification, which made motorized rotation practical, affordable, and convenient. Such was the fate of car windows, pencil sharpeners, and coffee grinders. In other cases, alternative designs arrived, such as lever-push or single-pull paper-towel dispensers. Goods that might have required cranking also changed: Now there is pre-ground coffee and pepper, and store-bought ice cream. Canned foods are still around, though many have pull-tab openers now, and many nonperishables come in packaging more convenient than cans. These changes turned in on themselves, too. Cheaper and lighter appliances have a tougher time standing up to cranking’s rotational force. So today, the crank is mostly vestigial, used for entertainment or diversion, as in the case of the restaurant pepper mill—or the tourist-trap penny press.

 Take a moment and mime cranking a device you remember. It probably feels unfamiliar. Your body stays put while your arm or hand moves in a circle. Considering the matter as I cranked my pool umbrellas closed, I felt a sense of loss in my low-crank lifestyle. Didn’t turning a crank allow me to govern action continuously with control and connection? I could speed up or slow down, actuating the mechanism to produce a precise outcome, couldn’t I? But now, instead: motors striving to get results .

 And yet, that sensation also risked turning me, an ever-aging man, into a proverbial crank. Those metal, hand-operated can openers were literally painful to use, I recalled. Symbolic delight is the only real benefit lost with the crank’s demise: Leaning across a front bench car seat and cranking the window down to address a love interest on the passenger-side sidewalk  just felt more romantic than pressing a button.

 I came to realize that the loss I sensed was not in the machines or their industry, but in myself. In my physical body. I simply do not rotate my arm in a circle much at all, anymore. That configuration of limbs and joints and muscles has hardly atrophied, but I no longer feel my body work in that way.

 I found this realization shocking. What other ordinary movements had I forgone or forgotten? So many. Sweeping my arm horizontally, as when writing longhand or returning a typewriter carriage; the vertical version of this act, as when working a water pump or sharpening a razor blade against a leather strop; tracing a finger along an arc, as when dialing a rotary telephone; rocking a foot up and down, in the manner required by a treadle sewing machine; riffling my fingers across a stack, as when searching a card catalog or fanning through a thick reference volume.

 When we miss the equipment of the past, I wonder whether we truly long for its outmoded company or rather for the version of ourselves that got to operate old tools. Nostalgia is in the head, and perhaps the heart, but something different lives in the bones and muscles, a weird gymnasium of forgotten gestures.

 I do not really miss striking matches instead of deploying a wand lighter, but I do miss flicking my thumb and forefinger and then cupping a hand over the flame, feeling the heat in the process. A no-touch forehead thermometer is far preferable to the mercury-filled glass version you put under your tongue, but now I find no opportunity to flick a wrist rapidly, as one did when shaking out the older device. I really do lament some obsolete gizmos for functional reasons. The heft of an old Western Electric telephone handset and the intimacy of its closeness to my mouth and ear come to mind—but even then, its disappearance is braided with more curious bodily absences, such as rotating my whole body to wrap in or unwrap from the long, coiled cord of the kitchen phone while talking to a friend.

 I found this discovery heartening. True, we can never recover the lost experience of the past’s defunct equipment. You will probably never hang up a phone hard again, or feel a VCR slurp a videocassette into its rectangular maw. Those times, and the implements that gave them texture, are gone.

 But your body is not. It has the same form and capacities (if slightly aged) as it did last year or last century. And your human anatomy is, generally speaking, exactly the same as the one enjoyed by your grandparents, or Gilded Age robber barons, or early-modern sea pirates, or ancient Mayan astronomers. Though it is harder to find reason to crank (or dial, or strike, or pedal), nothing is stopping you from doing so. Perhaps it even makes sense to own supposedly outmoded apparatuses just because they exercise those muscles—a crankable pepper grinder, for when you can’t get your hands on a penny press. To feel your body carry out forgotten gestures anew is even more pleasurable than the gestures on their own. Rediscovering them proves that they are not bygone, but obscured by the changes that made them rare.

 The Heft of Yogurt 

 My parents bought their first videocassette recorder in 1980 or so—unexpected, given that they were not early adopters of anything and VCRs were still expensive. When the device finally conked out in the late ’90s, I bought a replacement for $79, by my memory, from a stack on a supermarket-aisle end cap. By then, the VCR had become a commodity, akin to cereal.

 Dad was unimpressed with the new unit. “Crap,” he declared, as he picked up its small, featherlight form from atop the console television on which I had unboxed it. As with a wall-mounted telephone or a meat grinder bolted to a deli counter, the heft of an object can make it feel higher-quality. Even when a thing is never meant to be picked up and moved around, its weight and solidity contribute to the sensation of use.

 I’ve long been fascinated by the phenomenon psychologists call multimodal sense perception —the way we process the same sensory information differently when additional senses become involved. For example, when researchers served the same yogurt in bowls of different weights, they found that heavier bowls increased people’s perception of the density and overall appeal of the yogurt therein.

 Multimodal sense perception seems weird until you think about it for a moment. The “same” yogurt is not the same when it is served in a heavier bowl. It is changed by the act of eating it from that particular vessel. Of course it tastes different, because you are not just tasting it but also carrying it, or holding it. It’s not as if you would ever eat yogurt suspended in air, astronaut-style. In choosing serving vessels or flatware, you design a sensory experience bigger than its parts.

 That also means that cranking something you acquired just to give yourself something to crank—that pepper mill, say—will inevitably differ from cranking as an act of daily life, as when public-restroom towel dispensers required it. That’s okay, because it transports cranking (or whatever activity is at hand) somewhere new, where you rediscover the act in your body, in a new way and  at a new moment in time.

 Forgotten Gestures You Want to Reclaim 

 This month, I’d like to ask for your version of cranking. Is there a physical gesture that you remember doing often, perhaps in collaboration with a tool or maybe on its own, that has fallen by the wayside—but which you would like to reinvigorate? Or that you have found yourself keeping alive through a sustained, if modest, ritual? I’d love to hear about the small bodily actions you love, and the objects that become partners in carrying them out.

 Let us know in the comments. We may share your answer, including your first name and last initial, age, and/or location, with fellow readers in a future edition of this newsletter or on our website or social-media platforms.
